series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] mm: refactor find_next_best_node to find_next_best_node_in
series_items.patch_summary: The patch refactors the find_next_best_node() function to find_next_best_node_in(), which takes an explicit candidates nodemask, enabling building fallback lists with non-N_MEMORY candidates without changing the callers' behavior.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] mm/page_alloc: refactor build_node_zonelist() out of build_zonelists()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the build_zonelists() function in the Linux kernel's page allocation module to extract a new function, build_node_zonelist(), which constructs per-node fallback lists from candidate nodemasks. This change allows for building new zonelists from these nodemasks instead of just using the default N_MEMORY node state list. The patch does not introduce any functional changes and maintains the same behavior as before.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch refactors the zonelist constructors and iterators in the Linux kernel to make them more flexible and explicit. Specifically, it introduces a new function `find_next_best_node_in()` that takes an explicitly defined candidate set, and extracts the per-node construction loop from `build_zonelists()` into a separate function `build_node_zonelist()`. These changes allow for building zonelists over custom candidate sets and iterating them in fallback order. The patch is a refactoring effort with no functional change intended.

review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch without any objections or suggestions.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm/memory_hotplug: factor out node_is_memoryless()
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch refactors the memoryless node check in mm/memory_hotplug.c by extracting it into a separate function, node_is_memoryless(). The existing code is simplified and made more readable. No functional changes are introduced.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Raised a concern about potential races between node_spanned_pages() and ZONE_DEVICE memory hotplug, suggesting that the issue may be worth revisiting in a separate patch.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Sep 02, 2026 at 03:55:07PM -0400, Gregory Price wrote:
> A memoryless node neither spans present pages (populated or ZONE_DEVICE)
> nor has an offline-but-added memory block still linked to it in sysfs.
> 
> try_offline_node() presently open-codes this memoryless check.
> 
> Pull that into a node_is_memoryless() helper and pull the existing
> check_no_memblock_for_node_cb() helper ahead of the add/online path
> so it's clearer what is happening here.
> 
> No functional change.
> 
> Signed-off-by: Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net>
> ---
>  mm/memory_hotplug.c | 60 +++++++++++++++++++++++----------------------
>  1 file changed, 31 insertions(+), 29 deletions(-)
> 
> diff --git a/mm/memory_hotplug.c b/mm/memory_hotplug.c
> index 226ab9cb078ad..d0e94057682af 100644
> --- a/mm/memory_hotplug.c
> +++ b/mm/memory_hotplug.c
> @@ -1491,6 +1491,36 @@ static int create_altmaps_and_memory_blocks(int nid, struct memory_group *group,
>  	return ret;
>  }
>  
> +static int check_no_memblock_for_node_cb(struct memory_block *mem, void *arg)
> +{
> +	int nid = *(int *)arg;
> +
> +	/*
> +	 * If a memory block belongs to multiple nodes, the stored nid is not
> +	 * reliable. However, such blocks are always online (e.g., cannot get
> +	 * offlined) and, therefore, are still spanned by the node.
> +	 */
> +	return mem->nid == nid ? -EEXIST : 0;
> +}
> +
> +/* Caller must hold the memory hotplug lock for this check. */
> +static bool node_is_memoryless(int nid)
> +{
> +	/*
> +	 * A node still spanning pages (especially ZONE_DEVICE) is not
> +	 * memoryless.  A node spans memory after move_pfn_range_to_zone(),
> +	 * e.g. once a memory block has been onlined.
> +	 */
> +	if (node_spanned_pages(nid))
> +		return false;

browsing sashiko feedback:

[Severity: High]
This is a pre-existing issue and was not introduced by this patch, but can
this lockless read of node_spanned_pages() race with ZONE_DEVICE memory
hotplug?

---

This seems legit and worth addressing (other notes are addressible as
well, but this is maybe noteworthy).

I actually have some old patches sandbagged that tried to marry the
ZONE_DEVICE hotplug pattern through mm/memory_hotplug.c rather than its
separare entry-point.  Might be worth a revisit.

I don't know that I want to predicate this particular fix on this patch
but it's worth a think.

~Gregory

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/5] mm/mempolicy: add mempolicy_create()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function, mempolicy_create(), which creates and validates a memory policy without installing it into the current task's policy. The function takes mode, flags, and nodes as arguments, allocates a new policy, constrains it to the task's cpuset, and returns the policy or an error pointer on failure. This patch also exports the symbol for use in guest_memfd integration with KVM.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/5] mm/mempolicy: add mpol_set_shared_policy_range()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function mpol_set_shared_policy_range() that allows installing an already-built memory policy over an arbitrary page range without requiring a VMA. The existing mpol_set_shared_policy() function is reimplemented as a thin wrapper to derive the range from the VMA, allowing both functions to share a single underlying path. This change addresses limitations in the current implementation that make it unusable for binding entire backing inodes from in-kernel code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/5] KVM: guest_memfd: bind backing memory to a NUMA node at creation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new flag called GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE to the KVM guest memory file descriptor (memfd) feature. When this flag is set, the backing memory for the guest is bound to a specific NUMA node at creation time, rather than being allocated through a shared mempolicy that can be modified later. This change requires CONFIG_NUMA to be enabled and only allows binding to nodes within the calling task's cpuset. The policy is fixed for the life of the fd and cannot be rebound on later cpuset changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/5] selftests: KVM: guest_memfd: let the gmem_test() harness bind a node
series_items.patch_summary: This patch extends the create_guest_memfd() function to accept a node argument, allowing the gmem_test() harness to bind a node when creating a guest memory file descriptor. The BIND_NODE flag is used to determine whether the node argument should be ignored or used for binding. This change enables testing of GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE functionality.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/5] selftests: KVM: guest_memfd: test GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds tests for the GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE flag in KVM's guest_memfd feature. The tests cover various scenarios, including single and multi-node systems, invalid arguments, and edge cases such as non-zero padding and out-of-range node numbers. The tests ensure that the BIND_NODE flag behaves correctly when used with other flags and when faults occur on remote nodes.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces a new flag, GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE, to the KVM guest memory file descriptor (memfd) API. When set, this flag binds the backing memory of the memfd to a specific NUMA node, ensuring that all allocated folios are placed on that node. This is done by creating an MPOL_BIND policy for the requested node and installing it over the whole inode. The patch series includes preparatory work in the mm/mempolicy code, as well as selftest harness support and testing. The approach taken is to bind each fd to a single host node, rather than allowing interleaving across multiple nodes, which would defeat guest NUMA balancing decisions.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] mm/mempolicy: use SRCU for the weighted interleave state
series_items.patch_summary: This patch replaces the current implementation of weighted interleave state management in the Linux kernel's memory policy module with a new approach using SRCU (Schedulable RCU) to pin the global iw_table object and use it in-place. This change allows for more efficient handling of concurrent updates to the weights, reducing the need for synchronization and improving performance. The patch also introduces a new mechanism for retiring the weighted interleave state, which involves calling SRCU for sleeping readers and kfree_rcu for reference-less ones. The changes were tested with various configurations and tools, including KASAN, PROVE_LOCKING, and DEBUG_OBJECTS_RCU_HEAD.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] mm/mempolicy: stop copying the nodemask in the interleave paths
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes the unnecessary copying of a nodemask in interleave node selectors, which reduces memory usage and improves performance. The original copy was done to ensure consistency between the node count and the walk, but this is no longer necessary as bounds checking can be used instead. If an empty nodelist or weight is detected, the patch falls back to using numa_node_id(). This change affects several functions in the mm/mempolicy.c file, including weighted_interleave_nid() and interleave_nid(), which are used for allocating pages under a specific memory policy.

review_comments.author: Rakie Kim
review_comments.summary:
The reviewer pointed out that the patch's removal of read_once_policy_nodemask() may cause a potential issue in alloc_pages_bulk_weighted_interleave(), where the function derives per-node counts from a weight total summed over the mask, and a changing mask can make them exceed the request.

Reviewer Rakie Kim agreed that resolving the sleeping-allocation problem using SRCU is a better approach than patching the allocation site and removing copies from the fault path.

Reviewer Rakie Kim noted that after removing the nodemask copy, the loop bound in alloc_pages_bulk_weighted_interleave() no longer matches the actual mask being walked, which can cause the walk to stop short of the intended pages. They suggested counting nodes in the loop that sums weights, as done in weighted_interleave_nid(), to fix this issue.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hello Gregory,

Thanks for the series.

On Fri, 28 Aug 2026 21:59:43 -0400 Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:

---

I went through both patches. Resolving the sleeping-allocation
problem with SRCU rather than patching the allocation site, and
removing the copies from the fault path along the way, looks like
the right direction to me.

---

I have a minor comment on this part. After this change, everything
else reads pol->nodes fresh at the point of use - the weight sum
and the walk both look at the current mask. Only nnodes is still
the count from this earlier read. If the mask changes in between,
the loop bound no longer matches the mask the loop is actually
walking, so the walk can stop short of the pages the weight total
planned for. Would it be better to count the nodes in the loop
that sums the weights, the way weighted_interleave_nid() does it
in this patch?

	nnodes = 0;
	for_each_node_mask(node, pol->nodes) {
		weight_total += table ? table[node] : 1;
		nnodes++;
	}

[...snip...]

Thanks again for your time.

Rakie Kim

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch eliminates unnecessary copies of nodemask and node weights in the interleave paths of the Linux kernel's memory policy module. It achieves this by using SRCU to pin node weights in place, operating directly on pol->nodes for nodemasks, and clamping the walk to a single pass. The changes improve performance but may introduce a small trade-off in distribution accuracy during rebind operations.

review_comments.summary: Morton questioned whether a div-by-zero error is an acceptable way to report a bug when the caller passes in a weight of zero, suggesting that code changes might be needed.

On Wed, 2 Sep 2026 09:57:35 -0400 Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:

> On Wed, Sep 02, 2026 at 05:04:12PM +0800, Liu Jing wrote:
> > In alloc_pages_bulk_weighted_interleave(), if the iw_table contains
> > all-zero weights for every node in the policy nodemask, weight_total
> > sums to zero. The subsequent "rem_pages / weight_total" and

So if the caller passes in me->weight==0 then we consider that caller

In which case a div-by-zero is a perfectly acceptable way of reporting
